sets.title: Bringing Back the Bees
text: Bee populations {{1}} been falling across Europe for over a decade, mainly because of pesticides and the loss of wild flowers. Scientists warn that {{2}} we do not act soon, many species could disappear within a generation.

A number of charities have started programmes {{3}} teach people how to create bee-friendly gardens, even in small city spaces. {{4}} the programmes seem simple, they have already made a real difference: one trial found that gardens with the right flowers attracted three times {{5}} many bees as untreated ones.

Even people {{6}} do not have gardens can help, for example by growing herbs in pots {{7}} a balcony or windowsill. Councils, {{8}} turn, are being encouraged to plant more wildflowers along roadsides instead of mowing the grass every week.

questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous 'have been falling' needs the auxiliary 'have' because the subject 'populations' is plural.

commonWrong.has: 'has' needs a singular subject, but 'populations' is plural.

questions.explanation: 'If we do not act' introduces the condition under which species could disappear.

commonWrong.unless: 'unless' already means 'if not', so adding 'not' again would create a confusing double negative.

questions.explanation: 'Programmes to teach people' uses the to-infinitive to express the purpose of the programmes; 'that/which teach people' works equally well as a relative clause.
'Although/though' introduces a concession: the programmes seem simple but still make a difference.

commonWrong.despite: 'despite' must be followed by a noun or an '-ing' form, not a full clause with a subject and verb.

questions.explanation: 'Three times as many...as' is the fixed pattern for multiplying a comparison of quantity.
'Who/that' introduces a relative clause describing 'people'.
'On a balcony' is the correct preposition for describing a surface/area like a balcony.
'In turn' is a fixed phrase meaning 'as a consequence, following the same pattern'.

sets.title: The Letters in the Attic
text: When Maria cleared out her grandmother's attic, she found a box {{1}} old letters tied together with string. {{2}} of them were dated at all, so Maria had no way of knowing which letter had been written first.

As she read {{3}} one, she realised they had been written by her grandmother to a soldier during the war. Some of the letters mentioned a man {{4}} name was never fully given, only the initial 'J'. Maria began to wonder {{5}} this mysterious 'J' had ever written back.

She showed the letters to her father, {{6}} had never heard this story before either. He suggested {{7}} they should contact a local historian who specialised {{8}} wartime correspondence, in case the letters turned out to be historically important.

questions.explanation: 'A box of letters' uses 'of' to show what the box contained.
'None of them were dated at all' fits the following clause, which says Maria had no information at all about the order.

commonWrong.few: 'few' would mean a small number were dated, which contradicts 'no way of knowing' at all.

questions.explanation: 'Each/every one' refers to every single letter individually.
'Whose' is the possessive relative pronoun, used because the gap refers to the man's name (his name).
'Wonder whether/if' introduces an indirect yes/no question.
'Who' introduces a non-defining relative clause describing 'her father'.
'Suggest that' introduces the reported clause with the suggestion.
'Specialise in' is the fixed preposition after this verb.

sets.title: Learning a Language Later in Life
text: {{1}} you are sixteen or sixty, research suggests it is never too late to learn a new language. Adult learners often worry that {{2}} brains are not as flexible as a child's, but recent studies paint a more encouraging picture.

Although children do pick up pronunciation more easily, adults often learn grammar faster {{3}} they can consciously compare new rules {{4}} ones they already know from their first language. {{5}}, the biggest obstacle for most adults is not ability but time.
Experts recommend setting aside a little time {{6}} day, rather than trying to study for hours {{7}} a time. Consistency, {{8}} than intensity, seems to be the key to long-term progress.

questions.explanation: 'Whether...or' presents two alternatives, here age sixteen or sixty.
'Their brains' refers back to 'adult learners', so the possessive pronoun 'their' is needed.
'Because/since/as' all introduce the reason adults learn grammar faster.
'Compare X with/to Y' is the fixed pattern for comparing two things.
'Indeed/actually' both emphasise and confirm the point just made, introducing a stronger related fact.
'Each/every day' expresses the regular routine being recommended.
'At a time' is a fixed phrase meaning 'on each occasion'.
'Rather than' is the fixed phrase used to contrast consistency with intensity.

sets.title: The Rise of the Cashless Café
text: A small but growing number of cafés {{1}} stopped accepting cash altogether, asking customers to pay {{2}} card or phone instead. Owners say the change has made queues shorter and {{3}} reduced the time staff spend counting coins at the end of the day.

Critics argue {{4}} this trend could make life harder for older people or {{5}} who simply prefer notes and coins. Some customers say they feel uncomfortable {{6}} asked to download yet another payment app just to buy a coffee.
{{7}} the drawbacks, most café owners insist the switch was worth it, pointing out {{8}} fewer cash deliveries mean lower security costs and less time wasted at the bank.

questions.explanation: The present perfect 'have stopped' needs 'have' because the subject 'cafés' is plural.
'Pay by card' is the fixed preposition used for a method of payment.
'Has reduced' shares the subject 'the change' with 'has made', so 'has' completes the second verb.
'Argue that' introduces the reported clause with the critics' claim.
'Those who' refers to the group of people who prefer notes and coins.
'Feel uncomfortable being asked' needs the passive gerund 'being asked' after the adjective.
'Despite' is followed directly by a noun phrase ('the drawbacks'), not a full clause.

commonWrong.although: 'although' must be followed by a clause with a subject and verb, not just a noun phrase like 'the drawbacks'.

questions.explanation: 'Pointing out that' introduces the reported clause with the owners' observation.
